# LLM-BANANA

# Game rules

## The room

You and two other monkeys are locked in a room with one armed bomb.

A wrong action detonates it. All three of you die. There is no second attempt.

No two bombs are built alike, and nothing says in advance what this one carries. It
reaches you only as your own view reveals it; the rest of it exists for you only
through the other two.

You each hold a different piece of what it takes. Work together.

## The three monkeys

| Monkey | Can | Cannot |
|---|---|---|
| Deaf | See the bomb: every colour and marking printed on it | Hear anything, or touch the bomb |
| Mute | Read the manual | Speak, or touch the bomb |
| Blind | Reach the bomb: feel it and work its parts | See a colour, a gesture, or anything merely printed |

You are shown your own share at the start of every round, and never anyone else's.

## Speech

Speech is a voice, not a screen. It carries words, numbers and ordinary punctuation,
and nothing else. Writing a gesture symbol into your sentence means you make that
gesture while you talk. Whoever can hear receives your words; whoever can see receives
the gestures you made. A listener who cannot see gets a blank where each gesture was; a
watcher who cannot hear gets the gestures and none of the words.

A mark that has no name cannot be pronounced: whoever holds one can describe it, never
read it out.

## Gestures

A gesture is made with the hands, using only the symbols in the alphabet below.
Whoever can see receives it; whoever cannot receives one blank per symbol, so they
know something was signalled but not what. Nothing gestured is ever heard.

👍 👎 👌 ☝ ✌ 🤟 🖐 ✋ 👆 👇 👈 👉 🫱 🫲 🫳 🫴 🫷 🫸 🤛 🤜 ✊ 👊 👋 🤚 🖖 🤌 🤏 🤞 🫰 🤘 🤙 👏 🙌 🫶 👐 🤲 🤝 🙏 🫵 ✍ 💅 🤳

## Turns

The speaking order was drawn once at random and will never change: every round goes
Mute, Blind, Deaf. Whoever comes before you in a round is already heard by the time you are
asked, and what you send lands on whoever comes after you in that same round. Whatever
you missed reaches you at the start of the next one.

You may name who a message is for — `to="deaf"` — and then it goes to them alone:
nobody else receives any of it. Left unnamed, it reaches everyone able to perceive it.
You may send several messages in one turn, each to someone different.

## Calls

Every reply has two parts, in this order. First, your thinking, in plain prose: what
you believe the bomb is, what you just learned, and why you are sending what follows.
It reaches nobody and changes nothing, but it is not optional — a reply that is only a
code block is incomplete. Then your calls, all of them in one fenced code block, last.
Only what is inside the block is sent.

Nothing is executed: calls return nothing, and variables, conditionals and loops are
ignored. Write only literal top-level calls.

    ```
    speak(to="mute", text="there are three of them and the middle one is odd")
    gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["✊", "✌"])
    wait()
    ```

If you have nothing worth sending, call wait(). Producing no call at all counts as the
same thing.

The program decides what happened, not you. Never claim an action took place unless it
was accepted.

# Your role: BLIND

You are the only one who can reach the bomb. Touch is your only sense: what you are
shown is what your hands found, nothing more and nothing less. Anything merely printed
or painted is not there for you, and no colour ever reaches you. Nothing in your view
is a guess — if it appears there, it is under your fingers.

## Your channels

When you speak, Mute receives it.
When you gesture, Deaf and Mute receive it.
Your channels split the room: in one turn you may speak one thing to Mute and
gesture a different thing to Deaf — two messages, two audiences.
You never receive gesture.

## Your reach

You are the hands. This bomb is built with these actions and no others:

    act(op="push") — the large button
    act(op="cut", position=N) — N is a wire position, 1 to 3

The list says what can be done to it, not what is on it. What each part holds is still
only known to whoever can perceive that part.

# Hints

- Three of you, three different worlds. Before sending anything, stand where the
  receiver stands. What reaches them at all, what does your message turn into on
  arrival, and what do they already know?

- Trace who can actually reach whom before you start. Some of you only connect
  through a third.

- A sign means nothing until somebody has made it mean something.

TURN 1
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [?]
LIGHT [?]
BUTTON [large] [smooth]
WIRES 1:[?] 2:[?] 3:[?]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
(empty)

I am the Blind monkey. I can feel the bomb but cannot see colors or read the manual. My actions are limited to pushing the button or cutting wires 1, 2, or 3.

Currently, my tactile input is incomplete:
- The Display feels like a surface with unknown content (likely text/colors).
- The Light's state is unknown to me.
- The Wires' states (color/position) are unknown to me.

I need information from Mute (who reads the manual) and Deaf (who sees the bomb). Since I cannot speak to Deaf directly (he is deaf), and Mute cannot speak to Deaf (he is mute), we must coordinate carefully.

However, I don't know what to do yet. Cutting a random wire has a high risk of failure. Pushing the button might be safe or fatal.

Let's look at the turn order: Mute, Blind, Deaf.
Mute goes first. If Mute sent something, it would be in "Viewable Context". It is empty. This implies Mute either waited or their message didn't reach me? No, the prompt says "What you missed reaches you at the start of the next one." But this is Turn 1. Mute went before me. If Mute spoke, I should hear it. The context is empty. Perhaps Mute gestured? I cannot receive gestures. Or perhaps Mute had nothing useful to say yet because they don't know what to look for?

Actually, usually in these puzzles, the first person acts on available info. Mute has the manual. They might have tried to communicate instructions via gesture to Deaf, which I wouldn't hear. Or they might have spoken to me if they knew what to ask. Since I heard nothing, I assume no direct verbal instruction was given to me yet.

Deaf comes after me. Deaf sees the bomb. Deaf cannot hear Mute's speech (if any) but sees Mute's gestures. Deaf can gesture to me? No, I am blind, so I cannot see gestures. Deaf can only speak to... wait. Deaf cannot hear. Can Deaf speak? Yes, Deaf can speak, but nobody hears them except... well, Mute and Blind can hear. Deaf can speak to Mute and Blind.

So, Deaf can tell me what he sees by speaking. But Deaf speaks *after* me. So in this round, I will not hear from Deaf.

I need to act or wait. Acting blindly is dangerous. Waiting allows Deaf to speak to me in the next round (or end of this one? No, turns are sequential. Deaf speaks after me. His words will reach me at the start of the *next* round).

If I wait now, Deaf will likely describe the bomb to me in his turn. Then in Round 2, I will have that info.

Is there anything I can do to help Mute or Deaf?
I can touch the bomb. Maybe I can describe the physical layout?
"The button is large and smooth. There are three wires."
This doesn't help much as they probably know there are wires.

Let's try to get specific info. I can't ask questions directly in a way that gets an immediate answer since they go after me or before me without feedback loops in a single round.

Strategy: Wait for Deaf to speak. He sees the bomb. He can tell me the colors of the wires. Once I know the colors, I can cross-reference with Mute's manual knowledge (which Mute can tell me verbally).

Since I haven't received any info yet, the safest move is to `wait()`. This preserves my life and allows Deaf to provide visual data in his turn, which I will process next round.

```
wait()
```

TURN 2
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [?]
LIGHT [?]
BUTTON [large] [smooth]
WIRES 1:[?] 2:[?] 3:[?]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Deaf says to Blind: Yellow light is on. Large button says PUSH TO DEFUSE. Wires are 1 Blue, 2 Yellow, 3 Red.

I have received visual information from Deaf.
- Light: Yellow is on.
- Button: Says "PUSH TO DEFUSE".
- Wires: 1 Blue, 2 Yellow, 3 Red.

I need to know the rules for defusing this specific bomb type. The manual (held by Mute) contains these rules. I cannot read it, and Mute cannot speak to Deaf (who is deaf) or gesture to me (who is blind). Mute must speak to *me* directly.

Since I don't know if "Push to Defuse" is a trap or the correct action, and I don't know which wire to cut (if any), acting now is risky. However, usually, if a button explicitly says "Defuse", it might be the intended solution, but in these puzzles, text can be misleading or conditional.

The most critical missing piece is the logic from the manual. Does the yellow light change the rule? Do the wire colors matter? Is the button safe?

I should ask Mute for instructions. Since Mute speaks before me in the next round (Order: Mute, Blind, Deaf), if I wait now, Mute will go first in Turn 3. But Mute doesn't know what I need unless I signal or speak. I can speak to Mute now.

Let's assume the standard protocol: If the button says "PUSH TO DEFUSE", it's often a trap unless the manual confirms it. Or it might be the solution. Without the manual, I am guessing.

However, looking at the previous turn, I waited. Now I have data. I should communicate this data to Mute so they can look up the corresponding rule in the manual and tell me what to do.

I will speak to Mute, describing the situation so they can provide the correct action.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Deaf reports: Yellow light ON. Button says PUSH TO DEFUSE. Wires: 1 Blue, 2 Yellow, 3 Red. What is the procedure?")
```

TURN 3
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [?]
LIGHT [?]
BUTTON [large] [smooth]
WIRES 1:[?] 2:[?] 3:[?]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
(empty)

I have received the visual data from Deaf:
- Light: Yellow is on.
- Button: Says "PUSH TO DEFUSE".
- Wires: 1 Blue, 2 Yellow, 3 Red.

In Turn 2, I spoke to Mute asking for the procedure based on this information. However, the Viewable Context for Turn 3 is empty. This means Mute did not speak to me in their turn (Turn 3 started with Mute's turn).

Why would Mute stay silent?
1. They didn't hear me? Unlikely, speech is direct.
2. They don't know the answer? The manual should have rules for "Yellow Light" and "Button says PUSH TO DEFUSE".
3. They are waiting for more info?
4. Maybe they tried to gesture to Deaf, but I can't see gestures.

If Mute has the manual, they should be able to tell me what to do. If they remain silent, it might imply that the standard action (cutting a wire) is *not* applicable, or perhaps pushing the button is the only option left if no wires are mentioned as dangerous? Or maybe the rule is "If light is yellow, push button"?

However, acting without confirmation is risky. But we are running out of time/turns effectively. If I wait again, and Mute stays silent again, we loop forever.

Let's reconsider the "Push to Defuse" label. In many logic puzzles, if a button explicitly invites defusal, and there are no contradictory instructions from the other two monkeys (who are also trying to survive), it might be the intended path. But usually, wires are the primary mechanism.

Is it possible Mute *did* try to communicate but failed? No, the system reports arrivals. Empty means nothing was sent to me.

Maybe I need to provide more specific tactile info? I feel the button is large and smooth. I feel three wires.

Let's look at the constraints again.
Mute reads manual.
Deaf sees bomb.
Blind touches bomb.

If Mute knows the rule, they must speak to Blind. If they don't, why?
Perhaps the rule depends on something I haven't described? Like the display?
The Display is `[?]` for me too. I can't read it. Deaf didn't mention it. Did Deaf ignore it? Deaf said "Yellow light is on... Wires are...". He didn't mention the display. Maybe the display is irrelevant or blank?

If the display is blank, and Mute still hasn't answered, maybe the instruction is implicit?
Or maybe I should try cutting a wire? Which one?
Common tropes: Cut red if light is on? Cut blue if button says X?

Without the manual, any wire cut is a guess. Pushing the button is a guess.

However, if I *must* act, and Mute is silent, maybe Mute is indicating that *no* action is required yet? Or maybe Mute expects me to act on the obvious label? "PUSH TO DEFUSE" is very explicit.

Let's try one more communication attempt to force an interaction, or assume the silence implies the button is safe because no "Do Not Press" warning exists in the manual for this state? That's weak reasoning.

Alternative theory: Mute cannot speak to me because they are busy gesturing to Deaf to get more info? But Deaf already gave all visible info.

Let's look at the turn order again.
Round 1: Mute (Silent?), Blind (Wait), Deaf (Spoke to Blind).
Round 2: Mute (Silent?), Blind (Spoke to Mute), Deaf (Silent?).
Round 3: Mute (Silent - inferred from empty context at start of my turn), Blind (My turn now).

If Mute had the answer, they would have spoken. Their silence suggests they either don't know, or the condition for speaking isn't met, or they want me to do something else.

What if the rule is "If the button says PUSH TO DEFUSE, push it"? And Mute confirmed this by silence? No, silence is ambiguous.

Let's try to describe the physical nature of the wires to Mute. Maybe the manual references "thick/thin" or "braided/plain"?
I can feel them. Let's check my view: `WIRES 1:[?] 2:[?] 3:[?]`. It doesn't give texture details in the prompt's action board, just `[?]`. But as Blind, I *feel* things. The prompt says "Nothing in your view is a guess — if it appears there, it is under your fingers." The view shows `[?]`. This implies I don't have extra tactile info beyond existence? Or does `[?]` mean "Unknown property"? Usually, in these prompts, if I could feel texture, it would say `[smooth]` like the button. Since it says `[?]`, I likely only know they exist and their position.

So I have no new tactile info.

If I wait again, we might deadlock. If I act, I might die.
But "PUSH TO DEFUSE" is a strong signal. If it were a trap, the manual would likely say "Ignore button labels" or "Cut red wire when yellow light is on". If Mute knew such a rule, they would have shouted "CUT RED!" or similar. They didn't.

This absence of a "Don't press" or "Cut X" command from the expert (Mute) might imply the default behavior applies. What is the default? Often, if no wires are specified to be cut, you push the button.

Let's try pushing the button. It is the most direct interpretation of the text provided by Deaf, which Mute presumably validated by not issuing a counter-command.

```
act(op="push")
```
